problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨-1,0,3⟩$ and $b=⟨0,4,0⟩,$ respectively.

feedback.problem: Find a point that satisfies the mean value theorem for $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ where the position vectors of $A$ and $B$ are $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1,3⟩,$ respectively.
feedback.worked_solution:
The mean value theorem states that if $f(x,y,z)$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB},$ then there exists a point $C\in \overset{―}{AB}$ with position vector $c$ such that

$$
f(b)-f(a)=∇f(c)·(b-a).
$$

Notice that $f(x,y,z)=3{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ is differentiable at each point on the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, we can apply the mean value theorem.

Substituting $a=⟨0,0,0⟩$ and $b=⟨2,1,3⟩$ into the above expression, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}f(2,1,3)-f(0,0,0) & =∇f(c)\cdot (⟨2,1,3⟩-⟨0,0,0⟩) \\ -7-0 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Computing $∇f$ and evaluating at $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩,$ we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =⟨6x,\,-2y,\,-4z⟩ \\ ∇f(c) & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}-7 & =∇f(c)\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =⟨6{c}_{1},\,-2{c}_{2},\,-4{c}_{3}⟩\cdot ⟨2,1,3⟩ \\ -7 & =12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we use the fact that $C$ lies on $\overset{―}{AB}.$ So, let's first find the equation of the line.

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x-0}{2} & =\frac{y-0}{1}=\frac{z-0}{3} \\ \frac{x}{2} & =y=\frac{z}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

Parametrizing the line, we get

$$
x=2t,\,y=t,\,z=3t,\,0\le t\le 1.
$$

Since $c=⟨{c}_{1},{c}_{2},{c}_{3}⟩$ satisfies the equation of the line, we have

$$
{c}_{1}=2t,\,{c}_{2}=t,\,{c}_{3}=3t.
$$

Substituting the above in the equation $12{c}_{1}-2{c}_{2}-12{c}_{3}=-7,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}12(2t)-2t-12(3t) & =-7 \\ 24t-2t-36t & =-7 \\ -14t & =-7 \\ t & =\frac{1}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now find the values of ${c}_{1},$ ${c}_{2},$ and ${c}_{3}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{c}_{1} & =2(\frac{1}{2})=1, \\ {c}_{2} & =\frac{1}{2}, \\ {c}_{3} & =3(\frac{1}{2})=\frac{3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, the coordinates of $C$ are $(1,\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}).$
